name: Tomas Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Tomas. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the Kessler estate, twelve hundred acres of wheat, barley and sugar beet, plus about three hundred beef cattle being finished in the sheds. In winter I'm on the cattle, feeding, bedding, checking water. In summer I drive a grain trailer behind the combine or roll fields, and the big tractors already steer themselves with GPS.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the estate, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove parcel vans for nineteen years, then the depot cut routes and I fancied something different at 55. I'm the most junior man there, the farm manager still checks my work, and I'm on the bottom rate. Mira works mornings at the bakery, and with what we earn we've got maybe three weeks saved, so it's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, shame, I was enjoying it. At the estate I'd keep showing the lads the useful bits, like how I ask the chatbot to explain a fault code. Online I'd say the hype was silly, but the tool itself is handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much changes, which means still the bottom rate and three weeks saved. The estate is big and solid, so I'm not worried about the farm going under. I'm worried about the gap between what I earn and what a fridge costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying for my spray licence, which gets me a better hourly rate on the estate. I'm 58 and studying for a spray licence on my phone at the kitchen table, and my wife Mira thinks it's the funniest thing she's ever seen. I'd keep using AI every day to learn the jobs faster, the farm manager says I've picked up more in three years than some do in ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled, a bit impatient. I want to move up faster than the money lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the spray licence pay, in real terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a pound an hour more, maybe a bit over, plus I'd get the spraying overtime in spring. That's roughly fifteen hundred a year. For us, that's the difference between dreading the car service and not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would laugh at you for using AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerry, who's been there thirty years, calls it my little friend. But last month he asked me to ask it why the sprayer's boom kept dropping, and it was right about the hydraulic valve. He bought me a coffee and didn't mention it again.

say: I'd call the hype **silly** but the tool **handy**.
I'd keep showing the lads how I ask the chatbot to explain **fault codes**.
think: The estate is **solid**, so I'm not worried about it going under.
My worry is the gap between the **bottom rate** and what a fridge costs.
do: Finish my **spray licence**, worth about fifteen hundred a year.
Keep using AI **every day** to learn farm jobs faster.
feel: Fairly **settled** but **impatient** to move up faster.
S0.quote: I'm 58 and studying for a spray licence on my phone at the kitchen table, and my wife Mira thinks it's the funniest thing she's ever seen.
fieldNote: He uses AI daily as a **learning tool**, which wins over older colleagues.
His worry is **low pay**, not the estate's survival.
A spray licence is his **concrete** path to a better rate.

steps.text: Finish the spray licence this spring for a higher hourly rate
Use the chatbot daily to diagnose machine faults

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so learn it, and I'd say it to anyone. At the estate I'd tell the manager we should use AI for the field plans and the grain sales, it's already half there. Online I'd share stuff about free courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm well placed. The tractor on the Kessler estate already steers itself down the rows, and my job is mostly to sit there and not touch anything. The thinking side, the grain marketing and the ordering, that's the office's job, and they'll feel it before me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a drone pilot course this year, it's about six hundred and a few weekends, and I'd ask the estate to pay half. I'd offer to run the drone mapping of the beet fields, which they currently pay a contractor for. And I'd keep pushing my AI use at work, so I'm the one they ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good, a bit pressured. I've got to move faster than my age wants me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Six hundred is a lot with three weeks saved. Where does it come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the estate for half and put the rest on the card and pay it off over six months. Mira won't like that, she hates the card. But if it gets me off the bottom rate, it pays for itself in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else on the estate are you thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra in the office does the grain contracts and the payroll, and that's exactly on your list. She's been there twenty years. I'd feel bad being the one pushing the machines in while she's on her way out.

say: I'd say AI is **coming**, so people should **learn it**.
I'd push the estate manager to use AI for **field plans** and grain sales.
think: The tractor already **steers itself**, and my job is mostly to sit there.
The **office** jobs like grain marketing will feel this before my hands-on work.
do: Take a **drone pilot course**, about six hundred, and ask the estate to pay half.
Offer to run **drone mapping** of the beet fields instead of a contractor.
Keep using AI at work so I'm the **one they ask**.
feel: Mostly **good** but **pressured** to move faster than my age wants.
S1.quote: The tractor on the Kessler estate already steers itself down the rows, and my job is mostly to sit there and not touch anything.
fieldNote: He sees his hands-on role as safe for now and wants to **ride the change**.
He would **borrow** on a credit card to pay for training, which worries his wife.
He feels **guilty** that his push for machines may hurt Sandra in the office.

steps.text: Take a drone pilot course and ask the estate to pay half
Run drone mapping of the beet fields in place of the contractor
Use AI daily so the manager asks me about the new tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to move fast, and the government should pay for retraining at any age, not just for the young. At the estate I'd ask the manager to put me forward for whatever robots come. Online I'd share anything on robot technician courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the big tractors are halfway to robots already. On a big estate the robots arrive the first week they're cheaper than me, and I'm the cheapest person there, so they need to be very cheap. The planning going to AI in 2028 doesn't scare me, it's the robots in 2031, when I'm 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to get on a robot technician course, evenings, and to get to know the dealer in town who'd sell the machines. If the estate won't keep me, I'd apply to that dealer as a field technician, because someone has to drive out and fix them. I'd cut the car to one and save every bit I can, maybe seventy a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and pumped up at the same time. A bit like before a long drive in fog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Pavel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel drives lorries, and self-driving trucks are probably in this picture too. I'd tell him to get on a technician course with me, father and son, why not. He'd laugh, but he'd think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the dealer doesn't want a 61-year-old?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the estate and offer to look after their robots for less than a technician costs. I'm cheap, I'm known, I'm there already. It's not dignified, but it's honest.

say: I'd ask the government to pay for **retraining at any age**.
I'd ask the estate manager to put me forward for **whatever robots** come.
think: On a big estate the robots come the week they're **cheaper than me**.
Robots in **2031** hit when I'm 63, so that's my real deadline.
do: Start an evening **robot technician** course in the first year.
Apply to the **machinery dealer** in town as a field technician.
Sell one car and save about **seventy a month**.
feel: **Anxious** and **pumped up**, like before a long drive in fog.
S2.quote: On a big estate the robots arrive the first week they're cheaper than me, and I'm the cheapest person there, so they need to be very cheap.
fieldNote: He knows a big estate will adopt robots **early**, and he is the **cheapest** person there.
He uses the **three years** after AGI to train as a technician and court the dealer.
He would offer to work **cheap** to stay on, which shows how thin his options are.

steps.text: Start an evening robot technician course in the first year
Apply to the machinery dealer as a field technician
Sell one car and save about seventy a month
Urge Pavel to join the technician course too

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the sweet spot, enough time if you start now. At the estate I'd be the one volunteering to trial anything. Online I'd tell people my age not to give up on learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2034 means I'd be 66, so I've got time to get myself a role looking after machines and finish on that. The big worry isn't the job, it's money: the bottom rate and Mira's bakery hours, which could go when the bakery chain uses AI for ordering and scheduling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone and robot courses over two years, at my own pace. Spraying the neighbours' fields with a drone on Saturdays could pay for the boiler and the car without anyone's permission. I'd start with two or three neighbouring farms once I've got the licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, quite up for the rest of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could drone spraying bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small farm might pay a few hundred for a day's work, so maybe two or three thousand a year if I'm careful and the weather plays fair. The drone itself is the problem, they're expensive, so I'd rent one at first. I'd want the estate's blessing too, I'm not daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Mira's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's been at the bakery eleven years, but it's part of a chain, and the shifts are already planned by a computer. If AI takes the planning, they'll cut a morning person. I'd say she should ask about moving to the decorating side, which is all hands.

say: I'd call five years the **sweet spot** if you start now.
I'd tell people my age **not to give up** on learning.
think: Robots in **2034** come at 66, giving me time to **look after** machines.
Money is the worry, including Mira's **bakery hours** if the chain uses AI scheduling.
do: Do the **drone and robot** courses over two years.
Start **drone spraying** for two or three neighbouring farms on Saturdays.
Rent a drone at first rather than **buy** one.
feel: **Uneasy** about money, but **up for** the rest of it.
S3.quote: Spraying the neighbours' fields with a drone on Saturdays could pay for the boiler and the car without anyone's permission.
fieldNote: Five years lets him plan a **side income** from drone spraying as well as a technician role.
He's realistic about **costs**, renting before buying.
His wife's **bakery job** faces thinking AI first, which shifts the household risk.

steps.text: Complete drone and robot courses over two years
Spray neighbouring farms with a rented drone on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, and anyone who's paying attention can get ready. At the estate I'd keep being the AI person. Online I'd share how I learned it at 58, to show it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039 means I'm 71, so I'll be watching from the garden. The thinking AI by 2036 I'd love, it'd make the estate's planning better and maybe even my job easier. The money stays tight regardless, that's the honest bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the estate and keep learning, maybe the drone licence just for interest. Ten years is long enough for a 58-year-old delivery driver to become the man who knows the machines. I'd tell Pavel he's got time to change, but not time to waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm about the robots, the usual money itch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do the drone spraying side job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but slower, no rush. With ten years, I'd wait for the drones to get cheaper. That's the beauty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you worried in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the estate got sold to a big investment company, they'd automate faster than any farmer would. That's the thing that would change my mind. Not the computers, the owners.

say: I'd call ten years **generous** for anyone paying attention.
I'd share how I learned AI **at 58** to show it's possible.
think: Robots in **2039** come when I'm 71, long after I've stopped.
Money stays **tight** regardless of the robots.
do: Keep working on the estate and using **AI daily**.
Get a **drone licence** slowly, waiting for drones to get cheaper.
Tell Pavel he has **time to change**, not to waste.
feel: Pretty **calm** about robots, with the usual **money** itch.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for a 58-year-old delivery driver to become the man who knows the machines.
fieldNote: With a decade, he sees AI as **helpful**, and the robots arrive after he retires.
His real fear is the estate being sold to an **investment company** that automates fast.
Money stays **tight**, keeping him uneasy despite his optimism.

steps.text: Keep working the estate's cattle and grain carting
Keep using AI daily to learn new estate jobs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because a big estate would buy robots the week they're cheap, and I'd be 63 with three weeks saved. What would help is paid technician training for older workers, and an estate that offers the job of looking after the robots to the people already there.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people whether they want to be part of it. If the machines are coming anyway, I want to be the one holding the remote, not the one standing in the field watching.

headlineQuote: If the machines are coming anyway, I want to be the one holding the remote, not the one standing in the field watching.
portrait: Tomas is 58, a former **parcel van driver** now the most junior hand on a large arable and beef estate.
He and Mira, a part-time bakery worker, have about **three weeks** saved.
He uses **AI daily** to learn faster and wants to become the person who runs the machines.
He worries about **low pay** more than the estate, and fears a sale to an investment company.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious** because big estates adopt robots early, while slower pictures leave him uneasy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the estate would buy robots fast when he's 63.
whatWouldHelp: Estates offering **robot care** jobs to existing staff.
